paras: The lynching of Archer Cook was the killing of a Black man, about 22, whom armed and masked men took from the Prince Edward County jail at Farmville, Virginia, early on August 31, 1888, and hanged and shot. Cook had been jailed for months awaiting trial on a charge of assaulting a young white woman, Lizzie Frank. Wire items carried the news across the Midwest and the Dakotas, and a Leavenworth, Kansas, weekly addressed to Black readers urged them to arm and guard the jails.

On July 9, 1888, the Alexandria Gazette printed a Farmville dispatch saying that Miss Lizzie Frank, "a highly respectable young lady," had been "criminally assaulted" the previous Friday by "a colored man named Archer Cook," who was jailed. The Staunton Spectator reprinted it from the Lynchburg Virginian. According to the Gazette's later account, Frank was the daughter of "respectable German parents," and the trial had been postponed from term to term because she was too ill to testify. The Staunton Vindicator placed the alleged assault on a county road and said the trial was last put off the Thursday before the lynching.

The Farmville dispatch, dated September 1, said Cook was taken from his cell "early yesterday morning" by "a body of armed and masked men." They broke through the jail's brick walls, and the correspondent wrote that the affair was "managed as if by men drilled to this work." Cook "screamed piteously," the account continued, before he was hurried to the nearest woods and hanged from the limb of an oak with his feet touching the ground. At least twenty-five shots were heard, after which the men galloped off, leaving what the dispatch called "a terribly mangled corpse."

The Vindicator's shorter version said that "a mob of men" broke into the jail at dawn on Friday, carried Cook to the edge of town, hanged him and "filled his body with bullets." The National Tribune of Washington put the party at 40 armed men.
No report of an inquest, arrests or official inquiry appears in the coverage, and no paper named any of the lynchers.

In Virginia the lynching drew short notices. The Alexandria Gazette ran the Farmville dispatch under the head "Lynched," calling the alleged crime "a fiendish assault" and the lynchers "fearless and furious men." The Staunton Vindicator, in a column of items "gleaned from the mails," stated the assault as fact rather than as a charge.

Outside the state, a Richmond special said only that Cook "was lynched at Farmville today, for an assault on a young girl." A Wisconsin "Criminal" column described "a large band of masked and armed men" and called the accuser "a young and respectable German girl." Most widely reprinted was a sentence from syndicated weekly news summaries, "Archer Cook (colored) was hanged on the 31st ult. by a mob at Farmville, Va., for assaulting a white girl," which ran in Minnesota, Dakota and Wisconsin papers from September 5 to 15. The summaries set it beside legal executions in California and Texas, and the Chicago Citizen grouped all three under the headline "Choked to Death. Murderers Pay the Penalty for Their Crimes on the Gallows."

The Advocate of Leavenworth, Kansas, whose editorial column spoke directly to "colored" readers, took a different line on September 15. It called the killing "another outragous lynching" that "disgraced Virginia," noted that Cook was "charged with attempted assault," and objected that he was hanged and shot "without judge or jury." The paper told readers to "arm yourselves and guard the prisons night and day untill justice is prevailed," and in the same column counted 256 Black people lynched since July 1887, blaming the Democratic Party.

Accounts differ on several details. Most reports date the lynching to early Friday, August 31, while the National Tribune said Saturday morning. The Farmville correspondent said the men entered through the walls and used the nearest woods; the National Tribune said they broke down the doors, and it and the Vindicator placed the hanging at the edge of town. The Advocate called the charge attempted assault rather than assault; the Farmville dispatch, written in the town the next day, is the most detailed source.

accounts.label: Farmville dispatch
accounts.gist: Armed, masked men broke through the jail's brick walls, took Cook screaming to the nearest woods, hanged him from an oak with his feet touching the ground and fired at least 25 shots before galloping off.

accounts.label: Staunton Vindicator
accounts.gist: A mob broke into the jail at dawn Friday, carried Cook to the edge of town, hanged him and filled his body with bullets.

accounts.label: National Tribune
accounts.gist: Forty armed men broke down the jail doors on Saturday morning, hanged Cook to a tree on the outskirts of town and riddled the body with bullets.

accounts.label: Richmond wire and news summaries
accounts.gist: One-sentence reports that Cook (colored) was lynched or hanged by a mob at Farmville for an assault on a young or white girl.

accounts.label: Leavenworth Advocate
accounts.gist: Cook, charged with attempted assault, was hanged and riddled with bullets without judge or jury.

framing.detail: Alexandria Gazette, 'Lynched': calls the charge 'a fiendish assault' and the lynchers 'fearless and furious men' who acted 'as if by men drilled to this work', while recording that the prisoner 'screamed piteously'.
Staunton Vindicator states the assault as fact ('assaulted a young white girl') in a column of mail items, without comment.
Midwestern and Dakota weeklies ran a one-line summary, 'hanged on the 31st ult. by a mob ... for assaulting a white girl', beside legal executions.
The Chicago Citizen placed the wire sentence under 'Choked to Death. Murderers Pay the Penalty for Their Crimes on the Gallows', grouped with two legal hangings.

The Leavenworth Advocate, a paper in the white-press collection whose column addresses 'colored' readers, called it 'another outragous lynching' that 'disgraced Virginia' and urged armed guarding of jails.

conflicts.note: The Farmville dispatch dated Sept. 1 says 'early yesterday morning', and the Richmond special is dated Aug. 31; these local and earliest reports are the better evidence.
